title: hosted-api-stream-error-remediation-playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working PRD-style playbook focused on how the Hosted API surface and client SDKs should behave when streaming requests or tool-calls encounter partial failures, truncated output, or non-deterministic tool responses. The intention is to define: (1) a developer-friendly remediation model visible to integrators, (2) conservative SDK ergonomics that lower error-handling burden, and (3) telemetry and rollout signals to evaluate UX impact.

Problem statement (why this matters):
- Streaming clients and SDKs are the primary integration path for customers building real-time user experiences (autocomplete, progressive summaries, in-editor assistance). When an in-flight request fails mid-stream or a tool-call resolves inconsistently, app developers today must stitch retry logic, reconcile duplicate results, and handle partial JSON/structured output.
- These edge cases produce a lot of support noise: corrupted transcripts, UI flicker, duplicated side-effects (e.g., double-send to downstream services), and hard-to-debug customer issues.
- We lack an opinionated remediation model that spans the server runtime, transport protocol (stream frames), and SDK surface area. Without it, customers either implement ad-hoc hacks or accept brittle UX.

Goals:
1) Define a minimal, composable set of remediation primitives the server will emit during streaming and tool-call flows so SDKs and apps can respond automatically.
2) Provide default SDK behaviors that handle the common cases (soft resume, idempotent retry, visible remediation tokens) with clear opt-outs for advanced use.
3) Specify telemetry and experiment metrics to measure improved UX and reduced duplicate side-effects.
4) Create a staged rollout plan (beta SDKs -> opt-in runtime flag -> default-on) with backwards-compatible fallbacks.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not change core model semantics (generation continuity for non-streaming responses). It focuses on handling partial/truncated streams and tool-call side-effects.
- Not proposing a new binary protocol — we will reuse existing streaming frames with small extension fields.

User personas and key stories:
- Frontend engineer (mobile/web): wants the SDK to deliver usable partial text and gracefully resume without duplicate tool invocations when connectivity blips.
- Backend integrator: needs to guarantee idempotent actuation of side-effects (webhook, email) triggered by tool-calls.
- Solutions engineer: wants observability signals to triage customer-reported corrupted transcripts and to demonstrate fixed defects.

Core concepts / primitives (server + frames + SDK mapping):
1) Remediation token (remed_token): a short opaque string the runtime emits at stream start and associates with the request. It surfaces in streaming frames and tool-call responses. Clients use it to signal dedup/rollback semantics to the server on retry.
   - Properties: stable for the (attempt, request-id) lifecycle; rotates when the server explicitly cannot reconstruct prefix state.
2) Safe checkpoint frame (checkpoint): strengthens partial outputs by providing a server-signed checkpoint marker describing the accepted prefix, schema version, and last token index. A checkpoint allows clients to safely truncate UI and persist a consistent snapshot.
3) Partial-action markers (action-start / action-complete / action-abort): structured frames announcing tool-call boundaries. action-start includes tool id, idempotency-key (optional customer-supplied), and hinted side-effect scope. action-complete returns a canonical result id; action-abort includes reason codes (capacity/failure/timeout).
4) Resume hints (resumeable: true|false + resume_pos): when transient failures occur the server marks whether a given session can be resumed and the minimal resume_pos (token index) required.
5) Observability envelope: each remediation frame includes a small set of telemetry tags (backend-cluster, model-variant, attempt-id) to help correlate client-side retries with server logs.

Server behavior contract (high level):
- On stream start: emit remed_token and a pre-checkpoint baseline (if applicable).
- While streaming: periodically emit checkpoint frames at conservative intervals (defaults: every ~1s or every N tokens depending on latency profile).
- When a tool-call is invoked within a stream: emit action-start, then either action-complete or action-abort. If action-complete has not emitted and the connection fails, the server must store the action state for a short window (configurable; default 2 minutes) to allow idempotent retry.
- On transient internal failure: emit an abort frame with resumeable:true/false. If resumeable=true client SDKs can attempt resume; server will accept resume requests referencing remed_token and resume_pos.

SDK ergonomics (defaults we propose):
- High-level primitives added to SDKs: StreamSession (encapsulates remed_token, last_checkpoint_pos, pending-actions), Resume() API, SafeEmitCheckpointCallback, and ActionManager for tool-call lifecycle.
- Default semantics:
  * Soft resume: if the transport reconnects within the store window and server indicates resumeable, SDK attempts resume using remed_token and resume_pos. SDK merges new tokens into the buffered UI and emits a single checkpoint-consumption callback.
  * Action dedup: SDK will not re-emit action-start if action-complete has been previously observed for the same (remed_token, client-action-local-id). If the server returns a canonical result id after reconnection, SDK resolves promise with that result.
  * Visible remediation tokens: the SDK surface exposes a small set of hooks to clients: onCheckpoint(persistentSnapshotMeta), onActionAbort(actionMeta), onResumeAttempt(meta), onFinalized(prefix). These hooks default to no-op but are easy to wire into UI.
- Opt-out mode: advanced apps can disable soft resume and apply strict exactly-once semantics (server-assisted) by opting into action-confirmation flow documented below.

Action-confirmation flow (for strict side-effect guarantees):
- For critical operations, customer can pass explicit idempotency keys with action-start. The server stores the intent and returns an action-handle. Clients must call ConfirmAction(action-handle) after observing action-complete to instruct server to forward/commit side-effects. This defers destructive operations until explicit end-to-end confirmation.
- Tradeoff: higher latency for commit, stronger guarantee vs double side-effects.

API sketch (stream frames / JSON envelope examples):
- stream-start: {"type":"start","remed_token":"r_abc123","model":"x-large","seed_meta":"..."}
- checkpoint: {"type":"checkpoint","pos":432,"schema_v":"1.0","sig":"...","telemetry":["cluster-a","attempt:2"]}
- action-start: {"type":"action-start","tool":"send-email","client_action_id":"local-17","idempotency_key":"cust-453","hints":{"side_effect":"email"}}
- action-complete: {"type":"action-complete","tool":"send-email","result_id":"res_9f2","payload_summary":"sent to 1 recipient"}
- abort/resume: {"type":"abort","reason":"backend-timeout","resumeable":true,"resume_pos":430}

Note: SDKs will surface these as typed events and also provide a raw-frame fallback.

Telemetry and metrics (signals for rollout):
- Client-side metrics (collected by SDK): percent of streams that observed resumeable aborts, mean time to resume, % of sessions that relied on soft resume, frequency of action-abort, duplicate-action detections avoided (estimate).
- Server-side metrics: checkpoint emit latency, checkpoint persistence success, action-store hit rate on retry, correlation of remed_token to error budgets.
- SLOs and KPIs: reduce user-visible corrupted transcripts by 60% in first quarter after enabling default soft-resume; reduce duplicate side-effect incidents reported to CS by 80% for customers who opt into action-confirmation flow.

Rollout plan / experiment matrix:
- Phase 1 (alpha): runtime flag behind feature-flag; SDK beta (javascript + mobile) exposing hooks but disabled by default. Partner customers opt-in. Collect telemetry.
- Phase 2 (beta): enable soft resume by default in SDKs for non-critical action scopes. Action-confirmation flow remains opt-in for customers with side-effects. Add quickstart docs and test harness.
- Phase 3 (GA): default SDK behavior enabled; allow per-key account config for action-confirmation and checkpoint cadence.

Developer docs and diagnostics:
- Quickstart guide showing common integration patterns: (1) progressive UI with onCheckpoint -> persist draft, (2) handling action-abort to surface retry UI, (3) using ConfirmAction for transactional flows.
- Diagnostic tooling: a server-side remediation inspector page where support engineers can paste remed_token and view recent checkpoints, pending actions, and cluster logs. (Confluence + internal tooling).

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Default checkpoint cadence tuning: sample profiles (chat vs long generation) to propose sane defaults per model class.
- Retention window for pending actions (1m / 2m / 5m) — default 2m recommended but needs infra cost estimate.
- Wire format: keep JSON-framed streaming or introduce a compact binary for telemetry fields? Start with JSON extension to avoid fragmentation.
- Security: who can validate checkpoint signatures? We may need server-signed HMAC to ensure clients don't accept forged checkpoints in adversarial settings.

Risks:
- Increased server state (pending action store) may affect memory/DB at scale; mitigation: short retention and sampled persistence for non-critical scopes.
- Complexity in SDKs could produce new bugs; mitigation: start with small, well-tested JS SDK surface and mobile libs, run fuzz tests.
- UX confusion if remediation tokens surface too early or too often; mitigation: default to opaque tokens and provide high-level hooks that apps wire only if they want visible remediation.

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering: infra estimate for pending-action store; prototype server probe that emits remed_token + checkpoint for a small fraction of traffic (owner: Miguel Santos).
- SDK: implement StreamSession + Resume() prototype in JS SDK and mobile (owner: Asha Patel).
- Product: draft customer-facing docs and migration guidance (owner: Evan Chen).
- SRE/Observability: instrument telemetry keys and create dashboards (owner: Priya Rao).

Appendix: short integration example (pseudocode):
// JS SDK
const s = await Redwood.streamCreate({prompt: 'Summarize...'});
s.on('checkpoint', meta => persistDraft(meta));
s.on('action-start', a => showActionPendingUI(a.client_action_id));
s.on('action-complete', a => resolveActionPromise(a.result_id));
try { await s.resumeIfNeeded(); } catch (e) { showRetryBanner(); }

Closing note: this playbook trades a small amount of infrastructure state and protocol extension for dramatically simpler integration ergonomics and far fewer duplicated or corrupted end-user experiences. The pattern is intentionally conservative (opt-in for destructive flows) and designed to interoperate with existing tooling patterns. Feedback welcome — I'd like to get engineering estimates on storage and an initial JS SDK spike next quarter.
